catalog_quote: शब्द दगाड़ा हो जाता है। भाषण में अंतिम आ कभी लुप्त भी हो जाती है। क्योंकि गा पर स्वराघात होता है। ... २—कुमाउँनी में ह्रस्वत्व की प्रवृत्ति अधिक है। अंतिम स्वर प्रायः ह्रस्व हो जाता है। बोलने में प्रायः उसके स्थान पर अ रह जाता है। अतः शब्द के उपान्त्य स्वर पर बलात्मक स्वराघात होता है चाहे वह ह्रस्व हो या दीर्घ। जैसे भितेर, बैंणि, भिना, भुलि, चौंड़ो, च्याला आदि शब्दों में अंतिम स्वर लिखा तो अवश्य जाता है किन्तु भाषण में स्वर ध्वनि आधी रह जाती है या अ हो जाती है फलस्वरूप उपान्तय स्वर क्रमशः ए, ऐ, इ, उ, औ, आ पर बलात्मक स्वराघात होता है। ... ५—कुमाउँनी में यदि तीन स्वर ध्वनियों का शब्द हो और तीनों ह्रस्व हों तो बीच के स्वर पर स्वराघात होता है। जैसे–हि० खिचड़ी, ग० खिच्ड़ी, कु० खिचड़ि (च पर स्वराघात है)। कभी कभी तीन ह्रस्व स्वरों के शब्द में बीच का स्वर दीर्घ भी हो जाता है। जैसे—हिन्दी—भीतर। गढ़वाली—भितर। कुमाउँनी—भितेर।

new_statements.translation: 2. In Kumauni the tendency toward short vowels is stronger. The final vowel usually becomes short; in speech usually only a [ə] remains in its place. Therefore the dynamic (force) stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the word, whether that vowel is short or long. E.g. in bhiter, baiṇi, bhina, bhuli, chauṛo, cyālā etc. the final vowel is indeed written, but in speech the vowel sound is halved or becomes a; consequently the dynamic stress falls on the penultimate vowels e, ai, i, u, au, ā respectively. [...] 5. In Kumauni, if a word has three vowel sounds and all three are short, the stress falls on the middle vowel, e.g. Hindi khicṛī, Garhwali khicṛī, Kumauni khicaṛi (the stress is on ca).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (dynamic) in Kumauni falls on the penultimate syllable, a consequence of the reduction/whispering of word-final vowels; in trisyllables with all-short vowels the middle (= penultimate) syllable is stressed. Juyal adds that Kumauni stress is stronger than in Garhwali or Hindi and that it conditions vowel changes (e.g. dagaṛ > dagāṛ(a), G. dekhiyāl > K. dekhihāl).
new_statements.exceptions: Adjectives may take penult stress for intensification (miṭṭho), a tendency shared with Garhwali; vocative singular stresses the penultimate vowel; where a medial a is lost the preceding vowel is stressed/lengthened (G. kamlo : K. kāmlo). NOTE conflicting formulation elsewhere: Pandey 1977: 47-48 says stress 'generally falls on the first vowel of a word' (examples all disyllables, where first = penult), and Kandpal 2012: 102 cites a stress minimal pair bhasám 'walk hard' vs bhásam 'burn', implying at least marginal lexical contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statements about isolated/citation words in an impressionistic comparative (Garhwali vs Kumauni vs Hindi) Hindi-medium monograph; no dialect specified (implicitly standard/Almora Kumauni); sentence-level emphatic stress treated separately. Not an instrumental or phonemic analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Hindi sources describe 'Kumauni' generically, i.e. the standard/central (Khasparjiya, Almora) variety = kuma1273 at language level; Juyal's penult rule is explicitly tied to the western/central habit of reducing final vowels, which Grierson notes does NOT hold in Kumaiya (Kali Kumaun) and Nainital Kumauni where final vowels are preserved, so the rule may not extend to eastern dialects. Juyal 1967 is a Garhwali-Kumauni comparative work (the same file also sits under garh1243).

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the existing catalog statement (Juyal 1967: stress on the penultimate syllable) in wording, and agrees with Pandey 1977 (already held by the project: stress on the first vowel of the word). On disyllables the two readings coincide, so Juyal's own examples (bhiter, bainni, bhina, bhuli, chaunro, chyala) do not separate them; only longer words would. Same access limits as work 0: lending-only item, not reachable by automated download/403 on text; fragments from the full-text-search service.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sharma states, in passing, that Modern Kumauni (other than its eastern dialects) has initial accent, and that this initial accent is what elides final -o/-a and shortens the preceding vowel (jalo > jal, halo > hwal). The actual accent rule is in Part I sec. 23.2, which was not opened. Emphasis (not word stress) can be marked by stressing the penultimate syllable with consonant lengthening, or by a higher accent on the final vowel of the principal verb.
new_statements.exceptions: Eastern dialects (Kumaiya, Soryali; contiguous with Nepali) are excepted: they keep the final vowels, implying the initial-accent elision does not apply there. Emphatic stress on the penultimate syllable and terminal rising pitch in questions are sentence-level, not word-stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma's statement is restricted to Modern Kumauni excluding the eastern dialects (Kumaiya, Soryali), which keep final vowels; it therefore describes the central/western (standard, Almora-area) varieties. Juyal and Pandey write about Kumauni in general. Masica's stress section names no Kumauni variety.

readall_conflicts: Juyal 1967 (existing statement, Hindi) places the strong stress on the penultimate vowel of the written word, reasoning that the final vowel is shortened or lost; Sharma 1987 (Part II, snippet) says Modern Kumauni outside the eastern dialects has initial accent and that this accent elides final -o/-a; Pandey 1977 (held by the project from the earlier reading) says stress falls generally on the first vowel. Juyal's examples are all disyllabic, where penultimate = initial, so the disagreement is in the stated rule rather than in demonstrated data; Sharma's clause is incidental and the rule proper is in Part I sec. 23.2, which nobody has opened. Masica 1991 is silent on Kumauni (its nearest statement is 'weak initial stress' for Nepali).

sources.note: pp. 95-97 'svaraghat': dynamic stress is stronger in Central Pahari than Hindi and stronger in Kumauni than Garhwali; in Kumauni final vowels are shortened/reduced to [a] in speech, hence forceful stress falls on the PENULTIMATE vowel of the word whether short or long (bhiter, baini, bhina, bhuli, chauro, cyala); in a word of three short vowels stress is on the middle vowel (Ku. khicari, stress on ca); vocative sg. also stresses the penult (p. c. 6543 of scanned).
